scenes.text: How do two strangers agree on a secret when a spy hears every word?
In 1976, Diffie and Hellman published a way to do it. Think of it as mixing paint.
Alice and Bob share one public yellow. Secretly, Alice stirs in red and Bob stirs in blue. They swap pots in plain sight.
Alice and Bob each add their own secret again, and both pots match exactly. That colour is their key.
The spy mixes the two swapped pots and gets the wrong colour, with double the yellow.
Un-mixing a pot is the hard part. With today's whole-number keys, over six hundred digits long, nobody knows a fast way on ordinary computers.
